title: Index Maintenance, Bloat & REINDEX CONCURRENTLY
description: Detect index bloat, eliminate unused indexes, and rebuild corrupted indexes without blocking writes using REINDEX CONCURRENTLY.

data.text: Over time, heavy `UPDATE` and `DELETE` cycles cause **index bloat** (empty or sparse B-tree pages that cannot be recycled). Bloated indexes degrade query latency and consume excessive memory in `shared_buffers`.

data.title: Rebuilding Bloated Indexes Online
data.content: Rebuilding indexes without blocking application reads or writes.

data.text: Before rebuilding anything, measure. `pg_stat_user_indexes` reports how many times each index has been scanned since the last statistics reset, which exposes indexes that only add write cost. Comparing an index to its table size is a quick bloat signal.

data.title: Report unused and oversized indexes
data.content: The first query lists indexes that were never scanned; the second shows index size relative to its table.
data.code:
-- Indexes that have never been used
SELECT
    schemaname,
    relname   AS table_name,
    indexrelname AS index_name,
    idx_scan,
    pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(indexrelid)) AS index_size
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes
WHERE idx_scan = 0
  AND indexrelname NOT LIKE '%_pkey'
ORDER BY pg_relation_size(indexrelid) DESC;

-- Rebuild one index without blocking writes
REINDEX INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_customer_id;

data.title: CONCURRENTLY has caveats
data.text: `REINDEX ... CONCURRENTLY` and `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` do not take a long write lock, but they take longer, require extra disk space, and can leave an invalid index behind if they fail. Check `pg_index.indisvalid` afterward and drop and retry any invalid index. They also cannot run inside a transaction block, so tooling must issue them as standalone statements.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Index bloat slows queries by requiring more I/O pages to be traversed.
Use `REINDEX TABLE CONCURRENTLY` in production to defragment indexes without locks.
